Loving and Forgiving. þÿ Jean Paul Richter finely says : þÿ þÿ Man lias an unfortunate readiness, in the evil hour after receiving an affront, to draw together all the moon-spots on the other person into an outline ot shadow, and a night-piece, and to transform a single deed into a whole lite; and this only in order that lie may thoroughly relish the pleasure of being angry. In love, lie has fortunately the opposite faculty of crowding together all the light parts and rays of Us object into one focus, by means ot the burning glass of imagination, and letting Us sun burn without its spots; hut he too generally does this only when the beloved, and often censured, being is already beyond the skies. In order, however, that we should do tins sooner and oltener, we ought to act like Winckelmann, hut only in another way. As he, namely, set aside a particular halt-lmur ot each day tor the purpose of beholding and meditating on his too happy existence in Rome, so wc ought daily or weekly to dedicate and sanctity a solitary hour for the purpose of summing up the virtues ot our families, our wives, our children and our friends þÿ and viewing them in ibis beautiful crowded assemblage of their good qualities. And, indeed, we should do so lor this reason, that we may not forgive and love too late, when the beloved beings are already departed hence, and are beyond our þÿreach.

MACHINE FOR CLEANING BOOTS AND SHOES Machines for cleaning boots and shoes have long been in use in the, great hotels in the United States, and Mr. F. Ayckbourn has recently patented a machine of this kind in this country. He employs a lrame-work which supports a spindle, on which are placed one or more sets of concave brushes, and a small f eedbrush dipped into a contiguous trough siq plies the blacking. The spindle being put into revolution carries with it the annulus of brushes, and the shoes or boots being presented to the revolving brushes are cleansed, blacked and polished in an effectual manner, li is clear that in a machine of this kind the brushes maybe applied either externally or internally upon the revolving annulus, and the machine may be made to brush clothes as well as shoes, taking the precaution to employ different circles or brushes for the different purposes. The machine is put in motion by a band from a steam-engine, or other moving power.

It is all very well to begin a battle by throwing out skirmishers, but this is done upon the understanding that the first combitants have an army at their backs. Not many generals of whom we have any record would have attacked a huge organized force with a company of Riflemen. THE REVOLUTION IN CALIFORNIA By the City of Baltimore steam-ship, which arrived at Liverpool on Wednesday, and the screw steam-ship, Alp, which arrived mi Thursday, we have uews From New York to the bth inst. The most interesting intelligence is that relating to the policy which the Federal Government has adopted with reference to the revolution in California. On the 6th inst the President communicated to the Senate that lie had replied to a despatch from the Governor of California, who had asked for 3000 stand of arms, 2 mortars, 3C0 shells, and 2 guns of large calibre, with their ammunition and appliances. He likewise asked for the United States naval and military forces, to suppress the insurrection. This demand, by the advice of Mr. Cushing, the Attorney-General, the President refused to comply with, on the ground that the þÿGovernor s statement contained no information as to any act of resistance or obstruction having been offered to the constitution, laws, or official authority of the United States. Important Musical Invention. þÿ Mr. F. J. Julyan, of Gerrard-street, Soho-square, has invented and patented a new method of producing musical sounds, that will be the means of effecting great improvements in the construction of wind and stringed instruments. After making a great variety of experiments relating to the effect of wind upon musical strings; he has discovered a very simple and practicable means of causing strings aud wires iu a state of tension to vibrate without the agency of either percussion or friction, in fact without touching them. The motive power employed is a small current of air, either from the human mouth or a windchcst being made to impinge upon the string at one end of i, passing over the string and into a narrow slit or groove immediately under it, the groove being quite parallel to the string and extending onetenth along the length of it, leaving nine-tenths of the string available for fingering or attaching to a sound-board. The rapid alternate rarefaction and condensation of the air at the slit or mouthpiece performing a part the bow of a violin, and sustaining equivalent to the sound as long as the wind coutinucs to act upon it. We have seen it applied to a sound-board and organ-pipes; , and we have seen and heard an instrument made I upon this principle, called the Eolian Mono- 1 þÿ þÿchord, which has one bass string fifteen inches long, one end of which is fixed over a mouthpiece one and a half inch long, in the manner described above. It is held in the same position
as a flute and blown with the breath. Three chromatic octaves can be produced on this very simple instrument. The tones are of a peculiar kind and of excellent quality.

Steam Music. þÿ A few years ago (says the New York Times), the Rev. Dr. Dewey suggested the idea of converting the execrable noise occasioned by blowing off steam into soothiug music, so that instead of setting the teeth on edge and splitting the ears of everybody within a mile, it should have just the opposite effect of producing astute of quiet repose and harmonizing influence. The idea seemed fantastical enough, and yet we have lived to see it realized. An ingenious Yankee has invented an instrument which can bo applied to any ordinary steamengine, by which the escaping steam may be in.'ido to play a variety of lively or saddening tuues. The instrument is called the Calliope, and we yesterday heard it on the East River, giving out its wild aud wizard music on board the J steamer Union. The tones of the Calliope are rather screechy, it must be confessed, but they generals, one of them the Prince Royal ; nineteen I are sweet as þÿApollo s lute compared with the steam-whistle. Heard from a distance, the si rains come over the waves with a puzzling, weird and uncertain sound, as though a troupe of Tritons were blowing their horns, accompanied by a bevy of mermaids floating down the stream. We do not see why the Calliope may not prove

a very desirable addition to the steam-engines of packet ships to amuse the passengers. The only objection we can imagine to the instrument is that it might possibly divert the attention of the engineers and firemen, and so lead to an explo-ioti. Though the Calliope sounds so well a mile off, it may not be so agreeable on board the vessel where the music is made. Distance may be necessary to lend enchantment to the sound, and we rather imagine it is. There is one very great advantage which the Calliope would possess for sea-going steamers : two steam-ships passing each other at night might at least proclaim to each other their nation. Coffee-Leak as a Beverage. þÿ Why do we use the berries or beans of coffee for making a drinking beverage, while we only use the leaves of the tea-plant ? In Sumatra, prepared coffeeleaves, as stated in Professor þÿJohnston sþÿ Chemistry of Common þÿLife, is the only beverage of the people. A Mr. Ward, who resided in that country for a number of years, states that with þÿ little a boiled rice and an infusion of the coffeeleaf a man will support the labours of the ricefield for days and weeks successively, up to tho knees in mud, under a burning sun or drenching þÿrain. He states that he was induced to adopt it as his own daily beverage, and his practice was to take two cups of a strong infusion of it with milk in the evening, as a restorative after the business of the day. He found immediate relief from hunger and fatigue by its use. His bodily strength increased, and the mind was left clear and active. The natives ofSumntra prefer the leaf to the berry þÿ they believe it more nutritious, and they do not plant it for the bean, as is done in Brazil and Java. If the leaf of the coffee-plant is so excellent, let some of our merchants inspect, some of it, and give it at least a fair trial. þÿ Philadelphia Ledger.

Readers. þÿ There are four kinds of readers The first is like the hour-glass; and their reading being as the sand, it. runs in and runs out, and leaves not a vestige behind. A second is like the sponge, which imbibes everything, and returns it in nearly the same state, only a little dirtier. A third is like a jelly-bag, allowing all that is pure to pass away, and retaining only the refuse and the dregs. And the fourth is like the slaves in the diamond mines of Golconda, who, casting aside all that is worthless, retain only pure gems. þÿ Coleridge.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 5th SEPTEMBER, 1856. CHOLERA AT ST. THOMAS ! ! !

There are at the present moment so many conflicting reports and opinions afloat in our community in regard to the sanitory condition of the Island of St. Thomas, that we over here are really at a loss to venture an opinion of our own on the subject. We have before us the " Tidende" of the 27th and 30th ultimo ; from the former date we have made an extract, in which we find that the Board of Health had given it as their opinion that Clean Bills of Health could be issued to vessels taking their departure from St. Thomas þÿ and this opinion is said to have been arrived at " after sound and conclusive proof." In the same article our contemporary says " we rejoice that it is once more in our power to pronounce the Island perfectly healthy." The paper of the 30th not containing one single word relating to Cholera, the natural inference would surely be that the Island continued healthy. Whilst we do not desire to alarm our fellow-citizens þÿ nay, on the contrary, our hope rests on the other side, þÿ still we feel it a duty, a sacred obligation, to bring to the knowledge of our readers what we have heard and read in relation to the subject ; þÿ hence it is that we make the following brief extracts from private communications : one letter says: þÿ " We had a severe shock of Earthquake Thursday, 28th August, at 1 on o'clock forenoon ; unfortunately Cholera has re-appeared, and some respectable persons have died from it." Another letter, d?ted the 1st, from an equally reliable source, dolefully re-

lates that " Cholera is on the increase ; to-dav we have had many deaths within the hour." A third mentions the occurrence of the Earthquake on Friday, and continues that Cholera has been raging badly for the last few days. With these contrasting statements, we say, and without the aid of local official information, it is impossible for us to arrive at anything like a settled opinion. If the averment of the " Tidende" be correct, and Cholera has entirely disappeared, let us abolish quarantine, or, at least, reduce the period ; if, on the other hand, we may rely on private letters, let us then cotitinue to enforce those measures which, after Providence, in a manner have protected our Island from the awful scourge. Since writing the above remarks, we have learnt that a letter from St. Thomas states that on the 31st August there had been eight deaths, and on the following day about the same number. þÿ þÿ

From the St. Thomas Times, August 27. The opinions we ventured to advance in our last with respect to the sanitary state of the Island, we are pleased and grateful to find continues without alteration. The Board of Health, persuaded it would seem, that the distemper had positively disappeared, and having no longer any apprehension of its re-appearance, determined on Mondav afternoon last, to give as their opinion, that clean Bills of Health could, from that time, be issued to vessels taking their departure from this port. That the opinion thus given by the Board of Health has been arrived at after sound and conclusive proof taken by reviewing the circumstance from its numerous points, we have little hesitation in confirming; and that foreign ports to which vessels from this place may arrive with clean Bills ot Health now issued, will bestow lull and ample credence on them, we are also confident ; knowing, as s.aid foreign places do, how long the previous Board (instituted during the Cholera of 1853 þÿ t,) procrastinated before determining an opinion on the matter, and deterred its resolution for several weeks until fully satisfied it could with certainty recommend the issuing of clean Bills. The present Board has, in our opinion, been no less prudent, when we compare the difference between the first and last visitations, and we rejoice that it is once more in our power to pronounce the Island perfectly healthy.

On Thursday last about a minute before one o'clock, a very severe shock of Earthquake was felt in this Island. The motion is supposed to have been up and down, or perpendicular, and to have lasted a couple of seconds. There was no warning, rumbling noise in advance of the shock, as usual with most Earthquakes that have been felt here, but was sudden and powerfully oscillating, making the rafters and beams of houses to creek, as though by the action it would have shaken loose any matter offering resistance. Fortunately it was so brief in duration, or few buildings could have withstood its effects if continuing for half a minute. The earth however, did not indicate that agitation which was experienced here in the Earthquake of 8th February, 1843, that proved so calamitous to Point-a-Petre, Guadeloupe. It was strong, sensibly felt everywhere, and was quickly over. For these reasons it is thought, so to speak, that it was local, and had no connexion with any other place. It produced a very alarming effect on a number of persons, many of whom instantly fainted away, and have since continued unwell. A little girl is said to have immediately become insane, and remained so for several hours, but gradually returned to her former mind and is now restored. The streets were in a moment of time perfectly crowded with persons of all ages and sexes, who rushed from their stores and dwel-

From the London Weekly Dispatch. FRANCE. By way of celebrating the fete of the Emperor on the loth, 5s4 military prisoners have experienced the clemency of the Emperor Of these, the remission of the rem ainder of their sentence has been granted to 274. and the remaining 310 have had their periods of imprisonment reduced. The Eiuperor also, on the occasion of the same solemnity, has cxtenled his clemency to 493 civil prisoners, who had been poiuied out to bis Majesty's notice by the Minister of Justice as having acquired a claim to this indulgeuce from t.ieir repentance or fiom the situation of their families. Out of the above number, 240 have received full pardon, and the others have received commutations or reductions of their punishment. Ttie whole number of prisoners who have had their position thus ameliorated on the recommendation ot the Minister of Justice on the accouchement of the Empress, the baptism of the Prince Imperial and the fete of the Emperor, exceeds 2,300. The Monile.ur of Friday annouuees that on Thursday the Emperor received in a private audience Baron de Brunow, Envoy Extraoidinary of the Emperor of Russia, who, ou r lie part of his Sovereign, presented to His Majesty the Collar and the Order of St. Andrew Priuoe Gortsiiakoff, Commander-in-Chief of the Russian armies, and Captain Lisiansky, Aide-de-Camp of the Grand Duke Constantino, were also presented to his Majesty. Friday was the anniversary of the Einperor Napoleon's birth, in consequence of which no public busiuess was transacted, and tbe Bourse

was closed The day was kept as a general holiday, and vast numbers ot the people sought atnu.-emeut in various ways according to their own tastes and inclinations. The Emperor, accompanied by the Duke of Malukoff, was lo have reviewed some troops from the Crimea upon the occasion, but the ceremony was abandoned owing to the heat of the weather. This circumstance, however, created considerable disappointment, particularly as the atmosphere had become cooler since the counter-order was issued. Illuininations and fireworks closed the festivities of the day.

SPAIN. The Paris correspondent of the Times writes : " Senor Pacheco is positively appointed Minister to London. The fact of itself is not important. Senor Pacheco is a diplomatist of experience and a man of ability, who will, doubtless, worthily fulfil the not very difficult duties of his new post. But it is known that the Spanish legation in London was offered to Senor Olozaga, and even that he was strongly urged to accept it. His not having done so justifies the belief that he is not disposed to support the present Ministry, or to serve them in any capacity. This is the more significant, as we see by the papers that he has lately had interviews at Bayonne with several Progresistas of mark whom recent events have sent thither, and it must be accepted as a strong indication that there is little hope of an alliance between O'Donnell and the Liberals. According to reports, and to certain correspondence from Madrid, the liberty of the press is considerably restricted by the present Government, which, upon the other hand, is busy rewarding the

editors of the Vicalvarist journals, three of whom, it is stated upon pretty good authority, have been offered legations at foreign courts The precarious footing of the O'Donnell Ministry, and its want of popular sympathy and support, compel it, out of regard to its own safety and preservation, to keep persons out of Spain whom Espartero did not fear to admit. Thus it is that, Narvaez instead of acceptance of his ofter of services, was requested (or rather ordered) not to cross the frontier. Under the Progresista Government, although he was not invited to Madrid, where, indeed, his presence would have been injudicious, lie was at liberty, had 1 le chosen, to return to his residence in Andalusia. Gonzalez Bravo, a restless but not very dangerous political character, lived, harmless and unmolested, in Madrid, for a long time after the revolution of 1854, but he is now forbidden to enter Spain. Not a few others might he cited as in the same predicament. Various symptoms combine to show at once the weakness of the Government and the daily decline of liberty in Spain."

From the Illustrated London News. VULCANITE. In the Gallery of the Crystal Palace at Sydenham a suite of three apartments has been erected and furnished with the appliances of highly civilised life, nearly the whole of which, except some portions of the building, are manufactured in a new material, named by its discovever, Mr. C. Goodyear, "Vulcanite." The basis of this substance is lndiarubber, to which is imparted by a peculiar process several very valuable attributes, tending to exercise a beneficial influence in many important divisions of the arts and manufactures. This substance can be made to simulate plain or fancy woods; bronzes, as shown in medallions, or clear relief; ivory, buckhorn, and bone of every description, in which diamonds give and acquire additional brilliancy, ebony as applied to household furniture, either solid or veneered, to the formation of hollow ware, musical instruments, surgical, astronomical, and electric apparatus, the coating of firearms as a protection from rust, carriages and harness mountings, sheaths for swords, stalwart walking-sticks or the pliant dress or fancy canes, the backs of hairbrushes, combs, pens, everpointed and other pencils, and panels for oilpaintings, pictureframes, and an infinite variety of useful and ornamental articles. The material is as hard as, or harder than, iron, and will resist a heavy blow from a hammer without the slightest mark being left. With this quality of hardness it combines the facility of taking and retaining a beautiful polish. It will, moreover, resist heat up to 3U0

degrees; and with this salamandrine property, furniture may be almost said to be fire proof. Its ductility, while in process of manufacture, permits it to receive any description of pattern or form, and this must tend to place the best specimens of simple or elaborate ornamentation within t lie reach of most classes þÿ the more as the price of furniture thus constructed, and, it should be said, thus indestructible, will be considerably less than furniture of the ordinary kind. The specimens both of a quiet elegance, and the more ostentatious and florid, as shown at the Crystal Palace, afford us likewise proofs of the fitness of the material for chairs, sofas, bedsteads, couches, cabinets, escritoires, <Sc.c. In the latter the or-moulu and brass work is imitated by electroplating the material. Nor should we forget to mention that, while this furniture is free from injury arising from the carelessness of servants or other accidental causes, it possesses a thorough immunity from acid stains or marks from the placing of hot-water vessels upon its surface Its hardness, smoothness, and ductility have recommended it as an imperishable sheathing for ships' bottoms and the roofing of houses ; while the same qualities have induced the manufacturer to apply it to the formation offluttering fans for coquettish Belindas. That scientific world of mystery þÿ electricity, likewise pays tribute to this discovery; for, from the fact of the perfect isolation of Vulcanite, electrophones thus con-

structed give forth in dry weather a spark of some three inches in length. The power of resisting acids possessed by the Vulcanite suggests its value to the surgical and medical instrument maker; while its imperviousness to hot water and oils led Mr. Goodyear to mould all kinds of necked bottles, gunpowder-flasks, and other vessels, by

s T , G ft 0 I X a V I $U some of the many patents having reference to this discovery. Its application to all sorts of handles for knives and forks, and those of workmen's tools deserves more space than we can here afford, but it must be stated that the peculiar nature of the Vulcanite to resist percussion is manifested very convincingly in these handles of tools, as they may be struck either by a hammer or mallet without injury. And in the knives and forks the steel haft or prong becomes a permanent fixture; the handle being placed there while the material is j soft, it becomes, as the latter assumes the density and hardness of bone, a part of the handle itself, and may be plunged j into boiling water with impunity. Some | of the imitations of buckhorn, moulded | from the natural stag's antlers, are per- j feet, and when intermixed with pieces of the true horn, cannot be distinguished. Even the keeper of one of the Royal deer-parks has been sorely puzzled, and failed to select the real from the fictitious. Nor is the simulation of every other class of bone less marvellous. For book binding and picture-frames its importance is obvious, as the most ornate designs may be turned out as cheap as the most simple, and the additional i coating of one or more metals adds but slightly to the cost. The art of impart- j ing colour to this material is yet in its j infancy; but from what we have seen j we think it highly probable that many improvements, if not discoveries, will be made in this direction.

HONORARY REWARDS TO BRITISH j SEAMEN FROM THE PRESIDENT OF TIIE UNITED STATES, The following testimonials have recently been | forwarded by the President of the United States for presentation to British Seamen : þÿ A gold chronometer and chain to Captain R Wilson, and a tnedal each to George W. Blanohard, Geirge Finnis, George Lee, and William Lee, being respectively the Master and Seamen of the B.iti-a barque Sarah, of Belfast; and also a gold chronometer and chain to Captain Joseph Clark, of the British barque Balticola, of Liverpool. Mr. Dallas iu forwarding these presents acquaints Lord Clarendon that these testimonials are presented to the parties enumerated " in grateful acknowledgement for services rendered to American Seamen under circumstances communicated to his Government by the Consul of the United States at Liverpool." It appears that the American brig Crusader, Captain Joseph B. Wooster, with a orew consisting of M vster, two Mates, a Cook and four Seamen, sailed from Jacksonville, a port in Florida, on the 2 ird December 1855, laden with lumber and rosin, for Bordeaux, in France ; that on the 6th January she sprung a leak; and on the morning of the 10th January, while in a sinking state, and during a gale, she was fallen in with by the British barque Sarah. The Crusader's Crew did not suppose it possible for any boat to live in the sea then running fearfully high, and induced the Sarah to lie by thein. In the afternoon four of the Sarah's men volunteered for the undertaking, went in the boat to

the Crusader, and after pulling several times under her lee, finally afforded her Captain and one of her Crew an opportunity to leap into the boat. Becoming scared they returned to their vessel ; but encouraged by their own Captain, they renewed the effort and finally succeeded in rescuing all. The brave Seamen who manned the boat are the four above named to whom the medals are assigned. It appears also that the American schooner Mayflower, commanded by Captain Dupray, sailed from Georgetown, North Carolina, laden with lumber for Boston on the 30th December 1855. She was capsized on the 6th January, 1853, and her whole Crew perished except the Captain and two others These three were taken from the wreck by the direction of the Officer of the Baticola, and safely conveyed to Liverpool. Mr. Dallas concludes by saying that he " most respeotfully trusts that the Earl of Clarendon

will be good enough to cause these testimonials to be presented to the persons for whom they are intended accompanied by the thanks of the President of the United States, by whom their humane aud hazardous rescue of American Ma- riners from eminent peril is justly appreciated " þÿ if Mer. AMERICA. The Americans seem pleased that we have not retaliated for the Crampton dismissal, and their estimate of our good sense appears to be higher than before. We have not perceived any of the apprehended taunts about our fearing to assert our dignity; on the contrary, even the anti- English writers allow that in this matter we have displayed a manly bearing, almost worthy of Americans themselves. The excitement of the coming election, three months distant as it is, begins to be intense. The fight is between Fremont and Buchanan only, and the friends of each speak confidently, as usual in such cases. If our cousins adhere to their national character, they will elect Fremont, if only because he is a novelty þÿ Mr. Buchanan's smartness is a stale affair. Colonel Brooks, who committed the ruffianly assault on Sumner, has retired from the Senate, to get himself re-elected. The vote for his expulsion failed ; that is, there was a majority for it, but not the majority required. Ninety-five American senators were found to vote that such a man was a fit colleague for them. The jury could not agree in the case of the other senator who killed the waiter, but we are not told the point on which they differed ; there was no doubt as to the killing, and the waiter was not an article of property, being white. He was an Irishman, and was, perhaps, considered a middle term between slave and citizen, so the jury did not know what to do. Deeply we regret to record the last news from New York. It is doubly distressing, and

comprises the loss of a vessel on Lake Erie, with fifty lives, and the more hideous destruction of about a hundred poor children in the course of a holiday excursion by railway. The reckless wretch who þÿ the slaughter had poisoned himself. Illus- caused trated London News.

Russian Losses durino the War þÿ The total loss of the Russians, from the period of the passage of the Prutli up to the 1st of May last, amount', according to the official documents, as yet known, to 277,000 men cither killed on the field of battle or dead of disease. These losses must be apportioned among þÿ First, the first army of the Dauube, of which Marshal Paskiewitch took the command at the time of the siege of Silistria ; secondly, the first army of the Crimea under the orders of Prince Mensehikoff ; thirdly, the second army of the Crimea, commanded by Prince Gortschakoff ; fourthly, the two armies of Asia, under Generals Mouravieff and Bagration, which operated during two years in Armenia, and terminated their second campaign by the taking of Kars ; fifthly, the divers corps of the Sea of Azoff and the Dnieper. This estimate of the Russian losses, which is in great part based upon official reports and documents published in military journals of the country, is not at all beyond the bounds of probability, when we consider that Russia, obliged to defend the
southern extremity of her empire, was frequently obliged to order troops in the centre of her dominions to make forced marches of 10Q0 or 1200 kilometres

In port there has been nothing to deplore from the effects of the storm. On shore, unfortunately, the ease has been different. European Extracts. From the Illustrated London News. The affairs of the two Southern Peninsulas of Europe are becoming every day more critical, and more deeply interesting to the speculative observer. From Spain there is little to add since our last publication. Tranquillity reigns everywhere, and þÿO Donnellis still in supreme command ; so supreme and irresponsible that he does not even think it incumbent upon him to publish any explanations as to his future policy. This is a departure from engagements entered into no longer than a fortnight ago, when the coup d'etat was made. Then the people were assured that as soon as the country was tranquil the Government would issue a programme of its policy ; the country is now perfectly tranquil, helplessly quiescent, and all the þÿO Don- nell and his partisans vouchsafe to public ear of Spain is, that they have no programme to submit, and that they must be judged of by their acts. In short, all is simple Absolutism, with the direst forebodings for the channels into which the absolute authority may turn. Those who harboured a lingering hope that þÿO Donnell, once firmly seated in power, might revert to his former professions of Liberalism and Constitutionalism, will be disappointed. If Spain be ever destined to recover her liberties, it will be by the exercise of her own will, in a struggle more desperate, and at sacrifices more costly, than any she has yet experienced. And now, whilst apostacy and perjury reign triumphant at the Court of Madrid, Isabella II. seems disposed to revert to the traditional

policy of unscrupulous despots þÿ that of propitiating the Church of Home to sanctify and support her temporal authority. Monarchs of the old regime who assume to govern by Divine right are guilty of suicidal inconsistency when they deny the divinity of the only authority on earth which pretends to sanctify the claim. Despotism and Rome must go hand in hand together, dividing the honours and the spoils of government. Francis Joseph, the young Emperor of Austria, recently conceded to Rome all the important privileges which his ancestors in a struggle of four centuries had wrested from the grasping ambition of the Papacy. Ferdinand II. of Naples the other day prostrated himself at full length on the sea-shore at the feet of Pius IX., to renew as it were his feudal allegiance to the Papal See ; and now Isabella II., if report be well founded, is prepared to purchase the favours of his Holiness, by suspending or revoking the law of dtsamoriizacwn, one of the most beneficial acts of the Espartero and þÿO Donnell Government, and so sacrificing the interests and respectability of the state to the cupidity of the Church. If other rumours be true also, Holy Church is to be restored to her anci, nt and darling prerogative of guarding the souls of the faithful, and punishing those who fall into error in matters of doctrine. Spiritual persecution will thus again be brought in to aid the temporal power, as it was in the days of Ferdinand and the first Isabella. But can such a policy pos-

sibly long be successful in this the nineteenth century ? In Italy all is calm also ; but it is the calm which precedes a storm. Here we have various States, and various nationalities, each struggling under some peculiar form of tyranny ; all wanting but union of purpose to break their chains. Whilst Mazzini, with the impetuosity of one who cannot see difficulty or danger, calls upon Italians to rise as one man, cast out their oppressors, and declare their national will, Manin (a true but cautious patriot) advises a more moderate and temporising policy, which hopes even something from moral influence upon their rulers. We fear we cannot go along with him in attaching much importance to any concessions which Pius IX., or King Bomba might yield to conviction, unless backed by very significant external influences. Neither do we attach much importance to any suggestions coming from the Austrian Government, which at the utmost could lead but to a temporising and disingenuous policy. The hope of Italy is in the conduct of her sons ; and we rejoice to observe that some of their recent acts evince as much dignity as sound discretion. The Liberal party of Naples have re-

® T « ® 1 0 I I A V S $ « cently put forth a circular in which they exhort the people to prudence, to patience, and to the observance of a strict legality in all their proceedings ; and, appealing to the patriotism of the clergy and of the army, they fancy they foresee, through these means, an ultimate triumph of the national cause. Meantime the northern States of the Peninsula are nobly doing their part. It is here no insurrection of rabble, or battle of barricades, which threatens the oppressor but an authori- þÿ tative and dignified remonstrance on the part of the Municipal Councils of Ravenna and of Bologna, addressed to the Pope against the occupation of the country by foreign troops ; and demanding that the municipal law of 1850 should no longer remain a dead letter. Other municipalities will, doubtless, without delay, follow this noble example ; and result in a general pronunciamento, whi'h the Papal Government and its advisers can hardly avoid replying to. The Ravenne and Bolognese Councils have hit the right nail on the head ; and pointed out the only road to a solution of the Italian question. Let Italy be cleared of j would he foreign bayonets, and the Italians will soon settle their own affairs according to their merits. Pius IX. should not view this demand with alarm or repugnance ; þÿ it was the darling policy of Julius II., one of the most illustrious occupants of the Vatican.

From the New York Tribune. So far as the Sound Dues are concerned, they may be considered as definitively settled for the present, and probably for all future Administrations. The European Powers which were more directly and practically interested in wil- payment of those tolls were quite the ling we should bear tile brunt ol that controversy, while they stood aloof and avoided political complications which it involved, and yet anxious to enjoy any advantages that might result from our negotiations. Under these circumstances, and with the feeling manifested in the State upon giving the notice to terminate the treaty with Denmark, it was considered most prudent to abandon the discussion, and to allow that Power to claim the benefits which she has so long enjoyed. There is every reasonable probability that a commercial treaty will be concluded with Russia before the exodus of Gen. Pierce. During the war with the Allies, frequent overtures were made, offering liberal concessions, bfit Mr. M arcy declined to adopt them, being upright in maintaining a strict neutrality and unwilling to open any cause of exception to the Allies. Still the opportunities for conference, which then occurred, disclosed pretty freely the basis tint! general terms upon which a Convention might be formed, and peace has doubtless led to a more careful scrutiny of the exact conditions which are necessary for mutual advantages of trade. We have now nothing but an old treaty of friendship with Russia, which is

entirely unfitted to the present state of opinion, or to the relations existing between the two countries. England has heretofore monopolized the most valuable commerce between Russia and the United States, in manufactures, imports and shipping, by an indirect system which has levied a profitable tax tor agencies and factorage, beside the gams for converting our raw material into common fabrics, upon both countries. Remowal of the old restrictions, and direct trade, would turn into our exchequer annually many millions that now find their way into British pockets. The same thing is quite trueof Mexico, which, though adjoining our own Territory, has been in a manner shut out from commercial communication and free contact by a mistaken policy of exclusion, equally injurious to both parties. Her precious metals go past our ports to satisfy interest to British bondholders, and to pay for fabrics which might more readily and cheaply be supplied from the United States In the Senate, Mr. Clayton proposed a ten þÿyears contract at $16,680 the round trip, one trip per month, for carrving the mails to and from England. Mr. Herbert, one of the representatives of California, who has been acquitted of the charge of having killed an Irish waiter, has received notiee that he had better not make his appearance among his constituents again. Should he venture there he must make up his mind to face the Vigilance Committee, which does not bear much good will to him. His friends in the Senate, who do not seem half pleased at the way in which the people of San Francisco are carrying out " state-sovereignty" principles, have passed a resolution calling on the President "to communicate whatever information he might have respecting affairs in California with reference to the operations of the San Francisco Vigilance Committee, and whether application had been made by the Government of that state for aid in enforcing the laws adopted. Poor Pierce, sadly puzzled by the present portentous aspect of affairs, will find some difficulty giving satisfactory in a answer. If he say that he has done nothing, the Anti-Slavery men will ask him why he has been so ready to send the Government troops against the feeble settlers of Kansas, who never attempted to resist the authority of the Union, while be allows the Government to be set at defiance in California. It will be rather amusing to see how the President will explain the discrepancy. As for the Provisional Government of California, which still modestly calls itself the Vigilance Committee, it is now fairly installed in office, having put down the Government party by a coup dt main,

in which only one person was wounded The Sacramento correspondent of the New \ork Tribune gives the following account of the transaction : þÿ . þÿ Dr. Pettenkofer examined the localities of every important city in Buvaria visited by cholera, then the locality of each street, and at last tile condition of each house, in which examination lie was assisted by several other physicians and the police of the place. lie found that his observations agreed entirely with those made by the London physicians in 1S4S and þÿ 49, and with þÿJameson s report to the medical board at Bombay. Elevation and drainage are the best preventives against contagion, as the doctor illustrates by the official lists of mortality in each street and in each house, given in separate tables in his report. lie also shows, from the position of Wurzburg, Ratisbon, Forth, <$-e., that cholera never becomes epidemic in houses placed on a rocky foundation, and that sand underlayel with clay forms the worst basis on which buildings may be erected. þÿ Jameson, in his report, made a similar observation iu India, and observed þÿ that cholera docs not seem to be fond of þÿrocks. The London report, in like manner, shows the diminished mortality in elevated places ; but. it is the observation of Dr. Pettenkofer that elevation is the cause of greater health only when it facilitates drainage. Elevation, without drainage, affords no protection against cholera. This he proves by the progress of cholera iu Xuremhurg, lligansburg, and Freysing. On rocky or hard foundations the excrements of men and animals are carried off without being decomposed: while in loose sandy soil, especially

when underlaid with clay, they are infinitessimally divided and by the process of putressence in gaseous form again communicated to the atmosphere, to which they rise lighter than the liquid with which they are mixed. There is a specific germ of the disease iu all excrements proceeding from cholera patients, which is of course transferrable to any place to which the patient may move or be carried. The disease is not in the air, nor in the water , nor communicated by contact. The intensity of the disease in Munich, Augsburg and every other city examined by Dr. P., was in proportion to the drainage. The construction of the privies was iu nearly every instance the index to the malignity of the disease and the number of its victims. Courage and Tenderness. þÿ On the English face (says R. W. Emerson) are combined decision and nerve, with the fair complexion, blue eyes and open and florid aspect. Hence the love of truth, hence the sensibility, the fine perception and poetic construction. The tair Saxon man, with open front and honest meaning, domestic, affectionate, is not the wood out of which cannibal, or inquisitor, or assassin, is made, but he is moulded for law, lawful winner of the St. Croix Stakes to carry 10 lbs. i trade, civility, marriage, the nurture of children, for colleges, churches, charities and colonies. They are rather manly than warlike. When the war is over, the mask tails from the affectionate and domestic tastes, which make them women in kindness. This union of qualities is tabled in their national legend of þÿ Beauty and the þÿBeast, or, long helore, in the Greek legend of þÿ þÿHermaphrodite. The two sexes are co-present in the English mind. I apply to Britannia, queen of seas and colours, the words in which her latest novelist pourtrays her heroine : þÿ she is as mild as she is game, and as game as she is þÿmild. The English delight in the antagonism which combines in one person the extremes of courage and tenderness. Nelson, dying at Trafalgar, sends his love to LordCollingvvood, and like an innocent schoolboy that þÿ goes to lied, says, Kiss me, þÿHardy, and turns to sleep. Lord Collingwood, his comrade, was of a nature the most affectionate and domestic. Admiral þÿRodney s

figure approached to delicacy and efleininacy, and he declared himself very sensible to tear, which he surmounted only by considerations of honour and public duty. Clarendon says, the Duke of Buckingham was so modest and that some courput affronts on him, until they found that this modesty and was only a mask for tho most terrible determination. And Sir James Parry said, the other day, of Sir John Franklin, that, þÿ he if found Wellington Sound open, he explored it ; for he was a man who never turned his hack on a danger, yet of that tenderness, that he would brush nwnv a þÿmosquito. Even for their higliwaynu n the same virtue is claim-

as witissi inns pra donum, the gentlest thief. But thev i low where their war-dogs lie. Cromweli, Blake, Marlborough, Chatham, Nelson and Wellington are not tu he trifled with, and the brutal strength which lies at the bottom of society, the animal ferocity of the quays and cockpits, the bullies of the costermongers of Shoreditch, Sevendials and Spifaltields, they know how to wake up.

Of the Proceedings of the Burgher o Council of St. Croix. MONDAY, 29th SEPTEMBER, 1856, THE burgher council Held its Ordinary Meeting Members ,). Moore and C. Sarauvv prevented to meet. Following cases referred : þÿ Mr. Francis DuBois appeared, produced bis election-patent, and assumed his seat as member of the Council. Letters and communications from Government : þÿ Forwarding lor þÿCouncil d s eclaration a memorial from Miss Danielsen, tutress at þÿChristiansted school s for increase of salary, accompanied with the school þÿcommission s recommendation ; postponed. Forwarding extract of the proceedings of the rural school commission recommending that the instruction in sewing and writing as most irregular and expensive be at present discontinued ; but that hereafter $64 per month be allowed for salarying 8 females to assist the teachers during the whole of the school hours ; the commission considers the present instruction in needlework and writing cannot succeed, because it depends on the regular payment of lialfa-bit a week, which payment is not forthcoming, or stopped by the parents. Government suggests, that this disorder could be prevented by making the parents bind themselves for the said schooling lor a term of 3 or 0 months, the amount afterwards, if not paid voluntarily, to be enforced by the police, or otherwise, so that the planters, with the consent of the laborers, do retain the payment weekly out of their wages ; þÿ as a discontinuance of the

trifling payment now asked from them (involving the repeal of the school ordinance 15) would confirm the people in the habit of expecting everything to be done for them by the public. After some discussion, during which it was observed, that at any rate the instruction in writing need not depend on the appointment of female teachers, and that the gratuitous school instruction ought to be on the same footing in the towns and in the country, the case was left for further consideration and inquiry. Forwarding report from the Chief Inspector of Roads on the state of the bridge at Fair Plain, which requires a general repair, the cost according to estimate $689, say $354 for hardwood and $335 for masonwork &c., ; information has been received from the Chief Inspector that no reduction in the expenses can be obtained, þÿ that it is necessary that the work be commenced without delay, and that it is proposed that it be done by assessment on the estates in the quarter, double on those on whose road allotment the work is done. The Inspector as well as the Committee appointed arc of the opinion, that the expenses for the lumber be incurred by the Landtreasury, because the bridge is of greater benefit to the public in general than to the estates in þÿKing Quarter. s Government have approved of the immediate commencement of the masonwork by assessment on the estates in the quarter as proposed, but as regards the outlay of $335 Council is requested to forward its opinion. EDUCATION l is Kduc&tiou ft rins the coininou mind " There seems to he no subject on which there is so universal a concurrence among all enlightened communities as there exists regarding the vital importance of Education. We, therefore, take this opportunity to draw the attention of the Public to the announcement in to-day's paper of the Annual Examination to be held in the Danish .School in this town 011 Friday next, the 7th instant þÿ to which all interested in the well-doing of the youth ' of this Island are invited to attend. Without for a single moment attempting to question, the qualifications of the teachers of any school, yet, upon the broad principle, we may take occasion to mention our belief that a 'great deal þÿ infinitely all þÿ depends and rests upon the ability and watchfulness of the tutors employed ; and these, we imagine, cannot be secured unless the stipend be adequate to the responsibility. What individual, we ask, would relinquish other pursuits, and devote his or her time and talents to the mental improvement of the rising generation, unless fairly compensated, in order to place that individual above the smiles and favors of the Sons of Fortune. From a suitable and proper education, then, may naturally be expected a juster conception of duty to society, and a more happy and beneficial performance of this duty ; while, on the other hand, experience warns us that from ignorance we may look for nothing but disobedience and a perpetual ebullition of improper feelings.

Tut first fair contest between the Pro-Slavery party and the Free Soilers in the United States has been fought and won by the Southern slaveholders, who are, however, not greatly elated by their victory. From an analysis of the votes given by the New York Tribune , there does not appear to be much cause for rejoiciug. Out of one hundred and ninety-eight members of the House who were present at the final division, when the Array Rill was passed, ninety-seven Free State representatives voted for the Kansas proviso; while the majority against it was composed of eighty members from the Slave States, and twenty-one from the North. So far as this may be supposed to indicate the feeling of the electors throughout the Union it must give encouragement to the friends of Fremont. If the Northern and Western States concentrate their votes upon him there can he no chance for Buchanan. Other hopeful symptoms are apparent amidst the hubbub aud exaggeration of the Presidential contest. The German element, which has hitherto been Pro-Slavery, is now universally in favour of Fremont and freedom. During the last eight years several hundred thousands of expatriated Germans have sought a refuge in the United States, and, as the majority of them were Democrats in principle, they naturally joined the party which went by that name in the great Western Republic. Thanks to the Nnow- Nothing movement and the aggressive insolence of the South, the eyes of the Germans have been opened to the real character of the soi-disant

Democrats of America, and they are now the warmest friends of Fremont. Decker anil Struve, whose names will bo honourably remembered in connection with the attempted Revolutions of 1848 in Germany, have been drawn from their retirement by the momentous struggle now waging, and, in eloquent appeals to their fellowexiles, have abjured them, by their love of freedom and their hatred of despotism under every disguise, to rally round the Republican flag, and secure the return of a President who is pledged to maintain free speech aud to resist the extension of slavery Not less ominous for the domineering South is the newly-awakened interest among the various religious denominations throughout the Union in favour of Colonel Fremont. Till within the last few months no class of men has been more lukewarm in their opposition to the Slave Power than the Methodist, Presbyterian, and Congregational clergy in the Northern States. Sympathising too intimately with the wealthy and mercantile classes in their desire to maintain order at the expense of justice and humanity, they were always ready to lend their powerful aid in smothering every attempt to expose the evils which must flow from the aggressive policy of the South. Now, however, that the national conscience, not less than its sense of shame and degradation in the eyes of the world, has been thoroughly awakened, the clergymen of the leading religious bodies are coming forward en masse for Fremont. On former occasions they have either stood aloof or given their aid and

influence to the enemies of freedom Next November, we are told, they will be among the foremost and most determined opponents of Buchanan and the Border Ruffians, who seek to establish slavery in Kansas by brute force. From the Illustrated London News.) SCANDINAVIA. I DENMARK AND THE DUCHIES. Since the commencement of the late war against Russia down to the present day, on attention has mainly concentrated itself public the Danube, the Crimea, the Caucasus, the Euxine, the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. On these districts much historical and geographical knowledge has recently been accumulated, of great value in the discussion and settlement of questions relating to international policy ; but, for reasons presently to be assigned, it is highly desirable that accurate information should be circulated concerning the political position of Scandinavia. Under that compendious term are included Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Finmark. If we except Finland, it is only because it is incorporated with Russia. Schleswig is a Scandinavian duchy dependent on Denmark, as are also Holstein and Lauenburg ; but the two latter are portions of the Germanic Confederation. These distinctions are highly important, though they have been confounded by many publicists. To speak of Schleswig- Holstein as one and the same is to violate correct notions of ethnography, and to represent two inimical races as united in one common nationality ; yet this error lias been frequently committed. The interests and policy of Frederik VII. as King of Denmark and Duke of Schleswig, are purely Scandinavian ; as Duke of Holstein and Lauenburg he is a member of the Germanic Confederation, and in that character is represented in the Diet of Frankfort. In consequence of these double relations, his

position is peculiar and embarrassing. Should the Confederation declare war, lie is bound to furnish his contingent as Duke of Holstein, though as King of Denmark he may have pledged himself to neutrality, or even made a treaty offensive and defensive with the nation attacked by Germany ; thus the King and the Duke, that is Denmark and Holstein, may come into collision. Such is the anomalous position assigned to the Danish monarchy by the Treaty of Vienna, 1815. In earlier times some of the German Dukes had disputed the rights of the Kings of Denmark to the Duchy of Schleswig, but that controversy was settled in 1720 under the guarantee of France and England, when Schleswig was definitively incorporated with Denmark. According to JV1. Lallerstedt, Denmark Proper extended southwards to the Eider, and the German portion of the kingdom was included between the Eider and the Elbe. The Eider, from time immemorial, has been recognised as the true limit of the Scandinavian territory, and beyond it even Charlemagne never extended his conquests, nor indeed have any German invasions passed its banks. Tradition records that Charlemagne hurled his javelin into the river, exclaiming þÿ This is the limit of the þÿEmpire. Christian VIII., King of Denmark, who died on the 20th of January 1848, by an imprudent act, afforded a colourable pretext to the enemies of Scandinavian unity for carrying out their schemes of dismemberment. He appointed bis brother-in-law, the Prince of Noer,

brother to the Duke of Augustenburg, Governor of Schleswig and Holstein, thus giving to them the semblance of identity. Those Princes were of a German family, and entertained the ambitious hope of founding for themselves an independent State formed of the two Duchies ; hence arose dangerous intrigues, continued to the present hour, and fomented by Prussia, long desirous of becoming a naval Power. That desire, however, can never be realised, so long as she is confined to the Baltic ; hence she covets the possession of Kiel, an excellent ' þÿ Scandinavia , it Hopes and þÿFears. To compass these views the Court of Berlin sympathises with the Holsteiners and the disaffected in Schleswig in their agitation against Denmark, to embitter an antagonism between the Scandinavian and Germanic nationalities þÿ the object of Prussia being to use the Princes of Augustenburg as tools, with the ultimate design of seizing the Duchies for herself. These facts explain the cause of the late 1 war between Denmark and the Duchies, when the troops of the King of Prussia and of the Confederation invaded Schleswig and Jutland, under pretence of defending Holstein. On the 25tli August 1848, the armistice of Malnio was concluded between the King ot Denmark and the King of Prussia, in his own name, and in the name of the Germanic Confederation, but hostilities were soon resumed. While war was raging Frederik VII. redeemed the pledge he had given on ascending the throne, and granted to Denmark a constitution founded on universal suffrage. This compact between the Crown and the people was signed on the 5th January, 1849 ; but as Schleswig was still in revolt, it was not included, but a clause to this effect was inserted in the constitutional document : þÿ þÿ All that concerns the gevernment of the Duchy of Schleswig to be regulated after peace is þÿestablished. On Den- 5th July, 1850, the final treaty between the mark and Prussia was signed. Russia next interfered in Scandinavian politics by the pro-

tocol of Warsaw, dated 5th June 1851, and, although professing friendship for Denmark, supported the views of Austria and Prussia, flic members of the Germanic Confederation- as result of these negotiations or intrigues is thus described by Mr. Lallerstedt. The arrangement consisted in the granting of separate constitutions for the Duchies on the plans chosen by the Cabinets of Vienna and Berlin, and of one constitution common to all the monarchy, while Jutland and the Isles preserved the constitution of 1849. This complicated representation imagined by diplomacy, was full of snares. First, the incorporation of Schleswig into Denmark, for which Frederick \ The had with right taken arms, was condemned. II. patriot party of the Eiderists, who had so boldly was fended the rights of Scandinavian nationality, dedefeated. ... In the second place, the project of a common constitution introduced into the heart of the Scandinavian provinces the German elements which the Eiderists so justly misdoubted. They knew too well the encroaching spirit of Germanism, which, like a drop of oil, spreads where it touches. They saw in this pretented community an attack on Scandinavian! þÿ a perpetual war, under the appearance ol fraternity. The work of German diplomacy was doubly perfidious. While the Danes claimed union with Schleswig, they were separated from it by a constitution apart : while they refused any connection with Holstein beyond a personal union, they were joined to it by a common

constitution. Finally, the Danish party in Schleswig would be mutilated and weakened by the obstinate propagation of the German compact with Holstein ; Schleswig weakened by its separation trom Jutland ; and Holstein strengthened by all the influence of German royalty. The insurrection had been conquered by arms, yet it was made triumphant by diplomacy. The Cabinets of Germany were perfidious, that ol London was duped, and þÿI aris was blind. The succession to the throne of Denmark is one of the gravest questions of the luture, and its consequences ought to be well considered. To render this subject clear we must ascend the stream of history in the year 1397, when the union of Kalmar was proclaimed, by which Scandinavian unity was established ; Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, being then united under the sceptre of Queen Margaret þÿ called by some historians the Semiramis of the North, long before J the venal pen of Voltaire conferred that titie on J Catherine II. of Russia. At that period the Swedish nobles expelled their first King of Ger- I man race, Albert of Mccklenberg. Eric the j þÿI omeranian, successor to Margaret, was crowned with the title of King of the North, but ho was of German race ; and thus an early blow was ! given to the purely Scandinavian element, which ever since has produced fatal results. In course | of time the family of Oldenburg succeeded to the throne of Denmark and Norway, Sweden having l been previously detached from them, when it re- ! gained its national independence by the courage

of Gustavus Vasa, though at the expense of | Scandinavian unity. It was the Oldenburg faj lni'.y who brought to Deumark its right over j Schleswig and Holstein, of which they were the chief possessors ; and, in rcfercucc to tho latter j Duchy, implicated Denmark in the Germanic I Confederation. Now the Czars of Russia des-

cend from the Gottorp lino ol the ducal house ot Holstein, and belong to the younger branches of the house of Oldenburg ; and thus put forward a claim to intervene in the future succession to the throne of Denmark ; but that claim is really extinct. However, the subtlety of the Muscovite, now pretty well understood, and the tenacity with which the Czars cling even to shadowy preteusions, warns us to be on our guard against all eventualities. The extinction of Russian claims is thus shown by M, Lallerstedt : After the negotiations commenced by Catherine II with Christian VII., and terminated by the Grand Duke Paul at his majority, the hitter ceded llolstein- Gottorp, with his share and rights in the Duchy, to the King of Denmark, and further renounced, by the same act, all pretensions on Schleswig. As the price of ibis concession and renunciation Christian VII ceded to the Grand Duke the counties of Oldenburg and Delmenhorst, the present Grand Duchy of Oldenburg. The agreement was signed at the Castle of Kiel, the Kith November, 1773. Nothing was wanting to make this contract valid ; there was a reciprocal concession, and an exchange established by long after possession. Each was so entirely master, from that time, of the territories, mutually exchanged, that the Grand Duke Paul immediately ceded the Duchy ol Oldenburg, which lie had just received, to this relative, Bishop Frederick Augustus, of Lubeck ; thereby proving similar rig'' f-r 'he other contracting party in the t. rritory ot Holstein. It is well to insist on the

nature and terms of this contract, because in the new regulation of the Danish succession certain reservations made by the Czar are founded upon eventual rights which lie would have as Duke of Holstein þÿ rights which no longer belong to him. One of the constant habits ot Russian diplomacy is to slip a clause into treaties, which, though apparently unimportant, is intended to serve as the basis of great pretensions. This was the case in the Trea.y of London of the 8th May, 1852, for the regulation of the Danish succession, signed by the five great Powers and the King of Sweden. Scandinavian unity is essential to the maintenance of the balance ol power, and the more so since Russia has annexed Finland to her empire; nor are we to overlook or underrate the designs ot Prussia on the naval harbours of Kiel and Flensborg. Denmark, Sweden, and Norway united under one sceptre would form a strong outwork for the defence of Western Europe; and the dominion of the Czars over the Sound and Belts would prove scarcely less formidable than their occupation of the Dardanelles. England and France, prompted by the instinct of self-preservation, forgot their ancient quarrels and hatreds, and wisely united together to prevent Russia seizing the eastern key of the Mediterranean, and her armed vessels can no longer float on the Euxine, if the faith of treaties be respected. But treaties may be evaded, and the new steam navigation companies organised and organising, all whose ships are to be so constructed

as to carry guns (certainly not for defence against pirates) convey a hint that prudence will not disregard Russia, curbed in the East, will intrigue more stealthily in the north, and the Danish well succession gives her the opportunity. It lias been observed that the Straits of tho Sound, leading from the German Ocean to tho Baltic, give Denmark a position parallel to that of the Ottoman empire on the Sea of Marmora. If the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles have hindered the Russians from penetrating from the Black Sea into the Mediterranean, the Sound and the Belts offer no less an obstacle in the North. The Sound is a key no less valuable to Europe, shutting the Russian fleets out of the German Ocean. In this article we have not spoken ol Sweden, subsequent and early occasion. intending to offer some remarks We on that country on a shall then speak of Finland, how basely it was betrayed, and how cruelly its inhabitants have been treated by the Czars, who have violated all the contracts and engagements to which they solemnly had pledged their honour. We shall avail ourselves of the same opportunity to disclose the intrigues ol Russia to gain a maritime footing in Finmark, by constructing a deep-water harbour at Alten-Fiord, where impregnable forts might easily be constructed ; and offer some reflections on the policy of uniting the whole ot Scandinavia miller one monarchy.

þÿ v Iboriadlure. þÿ An agriculturist of Turn and Garonhc has recently put into practice a process for hastening the maturation of figs, which lias been crowned with complete success, and is now generally adopted iti the department. It consists in the application of a small drop of fine olive oil to the centre of the hud or eye of the lig. The oil is applied by means of a bit of straw, in such a maimer as to touch the

centre only. This operation should he made as soon as the hud or eye of the fig assumes a red colour, and in the evening after sunset. The lig, which was green, small, and hard before, appears on the following morning swollen, soft, and of a yellowish colour; the hud expands, and the fruit is gathered on the fourth morning, just as the seeds are being formed. By this process is obtained a fruit of a fragrance and flavour superior to that from natural maturation, and devoid of the numerous seeds generally so disagreeable in þÿfigs.

St. Croix, 7th November, 1856. Mr. Editor þÿ In the absence of news or other important matter, you may perhaps find room for the following questions relating to some of the imper

feet systems adopted by a great many of our Planters : þÿ VV hy, when our Planters complain of the scarcity ot Labour, do they waste so much \\ liy are carts loaded with hoes and trays, when forks and shovels will do it in one half of the time ! Why are all, generally two or three carts allowed to load in the pen at the same time, thereby occasioning confusion and loss of time Why is the manure thrown down in the field irrespective of quantity and distance between the heaps ? Why is the manure allowed to remain days and sometimes weeks exposed to the drying influence of a tropical sun and a stron" wind, before it is covered in ? \Y hy does the empty curt return t« the pen at as slow a pace as it is possible for ..nils to move ? Why is manure crooked out on flat and level estates, when carts properly loaded will carry out three times as much 1 Y\ hy are the plough mules generally extravagantly and over fed and the remainder allowed to be half-starved and neglected ! From the Illustrated London News.| The two great questions of European policy which at the present moment clamour for settlement at the hands of the men who in England and France aspire to the character of enlightened and far-seeing

ST. CROIX AVIS . statesmen are the questions of Naples and the Danubian Principalities. Insurrection is on the point of breaking out in various parts of Italy; and the Austrians, with a corps of 4000 men, have occupied Galat/.. Let the two facts, and all their causes and antecedents, lie considered together. The pressure of financial and monetary difficulties in France, with their natural action upon the commerce and finance ot this country, will, perhaps, induce the Emperor of the French to procrastinate the consideration of these two subjects, and lead t lie British Government to acquiescence in his views; but Italy and Moldo-Wallachia will continue, nevertheless, to be .stumblingblocks to the tranquillity of Europe. England and France are at tiiis moment reaping in difficulties the natural fruits of the shortsighted policy which dictated the Peace ot Paris, without securing a basis on which peace there were two enemies to confront; could securely rest. During the war þÿ Russia, to resist whose aggression we took up arms; and Austria, playing the part ot a liilsc friend, determined to make something out of the war, but who might have been bought if she could not be converted to honesty. Against Russia our weapons were swords and guns, and the stout hearts and hands of brave men. We did not use

have done, for we renounced the legitimate fruits of victory at the last moment, and dismissed with courtesy the foe whom we should have punished. Against Austria our weapons were those of diplomacy. II we had not to light, we had to treat with her; and we refrained from doing so. For the rich bribe of the Dauubian Principalities, upon which she has set her dishonest soul, she would, if properly urged, have given up Lombardy and Venice ; and Turkey, deprived of those provinces, would perhaps have been content with Bessarabia, Georgia, and the Crimea, which, it the Allies had pleased, they could have wrested from the present possessor, and handed over to the original proprietor. But neither of these things was done. Italy and its wants were ignored. The question ol the Danuhian Principalities was left to the chapter of accidents. The Austriaus were allowed to remain in possession till the very name of an Austrian stank in the nostrils of Moldavians and Wallachians. At the present moment public feeling in the Principalities is so exasperated that 110 possible rearrangement of the European system would induce the Moldo-Wallachians to tolerate their annexation to the heterogeneous and detested empire ot Francis Joseph. We see already a few of the complications, contradictions, and vexations which this absence of high principle 011 the part of Great Britain and France has brought into the actual condition of Europe. Their threatened intervention in the affairs ot Naples is resisted by Russia þÿ and very

properly, considering why war was made against herself in the Crimea. It is also resisted by Austria þÿ the Power whose intervention in tiivour of the Pope against his own subjects, and in Lucca and Parma, against the Liberal party in Italy, ot Sar- more especially against the King and dinia, is one of the most glaring violations of the principle of non-intervention which it is possible to conceive. Austria, through article in the Journal (le Franc for I , warns Great Britain and France against interference in Italy. Why should not Great Britain and France take her at her word? Why should not they reply " We will not interfere in Italy, neither shall you" ? This might he done, it Great Britain were the only opponent of Austrian policy ; but, for good or for evil, this fortunes try has linked itself to the personal coun-

of the Emperor Napoleon, and cauot reply to Austria as justice and sound logic would dictate. The consequence is, that the two great nations which stand at the head ot modern civilisation find themselves in a false position. Both of them know the right course ; and one of the two, though willing to pursue it, is united with an ally who has selfish objects, incompatible with a just and comprehensive policy. We interfere to achieve the constitutional freedom of the Neapolitans, and Sicilians þÿ a result which is not worth achieving, if it is to he accompanied by the subjugation of Rome, and of the Lombardo-Veuetiau provinces. And to combat revolution in Italy, which we have no reason to fear, we lend ourselves to measures which have no purpose but to preserve the status quo, which, as far as this country is concerned, is cither not worth preserving, or is so little a business of ours that t he interruption of the status qua, and the remodelling of the map ol Italy, would be to us, and to all Powers interested in the permanent peace of Europe, a matter of positive advantage. In the case of the Danubiau Principalities there is the same unworthy and dangerous truckling to Austria 011 the part of France and England. What is Austria to England, or England to Austria, that we should be afraid of her 1 What is Austria to France, that France þÿ so powerful, so highly-placed, and so strong in herself- þÿ should defer to the exigencies ol the Kaiser '< It Austria fell to pieces to-morrow, Europe and liutna-

nitv would exist all the same; and perhaps Europe and humanity would be all the better for the collapse. To meddle with such a paltry' potentate as the Kinir ot Naples i- mere make-believe and sham, while we leave such a monster offender as the Emperor of Austria, unchallenged and undisturbed. To tell Ferdinand to amend the evil of his ways in Naples, and to leave Francis Joseph 111 unprotested possession of Moldo-Wallachia, is unworthy of Powers who have assumed the high duties and responsibilities of Great Britain and France. If these Powers are to keep the peace of Europe, let them begin with the great disturbers. When these are taught reason þÿ either by fear or by any other agencies þÿ the little offenders will cease to give them trouble.

Moldavia During the occupation of the Danubiau provinces by the " Austrians, 100 officers of the corps of geographical engineers," assisted by several foreign officers, were charged to make the trigonometrical survey of those provinces. The surveys tend to show the importance of the territorial concession made by Russia. In execution of the treaty of Paris of the 30th March last, that Power restores to Moldavia a part of Bessarabia, which comprises 1,125,000 superficial hectares (the hectare is nearly 2i acres). Moldavia, which formerly contained 4,720,000 hectares, will henceforth consist of 5,845,000. It will be as large as Bohemia, as Greece with the Ionian Isles, as the kingdom of Saxony, and much larger than Belgium. The portion of Bessarabia which the Russians have ceded is not the nmst fertile, but contains the banks of the Danube and five towns, three of which are ports, þÿ K ilia, Ismail, and Reni, ol veritable political commercial, and strategical importance. At present by the treaty of Paris, Moldavia will be restored to six-tenths of what she was at lite period of Iter greatest power, and her population will be increased bv about IO.OUO souls.

Yesterday afternoon an experiment was made at Manchester, in the presence of a number of scientific gentlemen, to test an invention to prevent steam-boiler explosions. The trial took place at the works of the patentee, Mr. William Ifoutledge, Newbridge Brass Foundry. The apparatus,

sists of an elbow pipe connecting the furnace with the side flue, and is fixed just below the water level in the boiler, but may be fixed at any elevation, or in question perfectly legal, any position requisite, and can be applied to any kind of boiler, as an opening into a side or centre flue .is all that is required. This pipe is perforated with a number of holes, about half an inch diameter, so placed as to be subject to the immediate action of the furnace fire. In these holes ure metal plugs, more or less fusible, according to the working pressure of the boiler. The moment the water in the boiler, from neglect or otherwise, is below the level, and leaves this pipe bare, the heat from the furnace acts upon the plugs, which melt, and the steam, escaping through the holes, immediately relieves the pressure in the boiler, and in a short time extinguishes the furnace fire, thus preventing at the once bursting of boiler the possibility ot the from want of water, or injury to the boiler from the action of the tire upon the plates bare of water, which latter cause so frequently results in ultimate accident and loss of life. The experiment tried on this occasion was very successful. In less than one minute after the water was let off, so its to leave the pipe in the boiler just bare, the plugs melted away, and the steam escaped through the holes. The pressure of steam the boiler at the moment was 40 lbs., and in about 10 minutes it was down to 2-5 lb. There was no inconvenience caused
in the furnace, as the steam, after acting for a few moments upon the fire, can be turned off through the regular þÿchannel. English Paper.

COMETS. þÿl rof.Stephen Alexander read a paper ou the Physical Peculiarities of Comets, of which the substance was as follows:- þÿ He first remarked upon the close association of the imponderable substances, and drew the conclusion that, as the sun is very hot, and being bright, and also now proved to be magnetic, he must also be highly electrified. He found in this electricity the cause ol the repulsive energy which Bessell and Gausss have shown to be necessary to account for the form of the þÿcomet head. s The tail was regarded as matter centinually thrown off by electrical repulsion. The curvature of the tail was accounted lor by the change in the direction of the þÿcomet s motion while the tail was developed. The elongation and subsequent rupture of þÿBicla comet s was referred to an intense induction ; the rupture occurring, of course, in the region of most feeble cohesion, away from the sun. An arch of cometary matter, however, remained, through which discharges of electricity must have taken place, as the two portions thus tied become unequally electrified : sometimes rendering the one portion of the comet the more conspicuous and sometimes the other, as was observed. These discharges subsequently ruptured the arch and the comet divided into two, which have since returned separate.

TIIE YELLOW FEVER. ON THE METEOROLOGICAL PHENOMENA DURING THE EPIDEMIC OF 1855, AT PORTSMOUTH VA , BY NATHAN B. WEBSTER. 'I'he meteorological daia of this paper were obtained by permission ot the Navy Department, from the log of the receiving ship at the Norfolk station, during the months of July, August, Sep tember and October, 1855. On these data a chart was prepared hy Professor Webster, which was exhibited to the section, representing at a glance the results of more than two thousand observations. The mean temperature for each day was shown by a curve, the ordinates being drawn on a scale of eight degrees of the thermometer to one inch. The atmospheric pressure was also shown by a curve through points indicated by the barometer. The cloudiness was indicated by suitable symbols, as also the electrical phenomena and direction of the wind. The daily mortality was shown hy a curve made on a scale of eight deaths to one inch on the ordinates, thus exhibiting to the eye the actual relations of the weather and mortality. The red curve of temperature seemed to correspond in parallelism with the black curve of mortality, while the blue curve of atmospheric pressure almost invariably descended just previous to an increase of deaths The instances of thut.dcr anJ lightning were rare during the summer, no instance appearing after the 13th of September, and usually occurring subsequent, to increased mortality The wind duiing July w is mostly from the southwest, sometimes a week in succession without change

LEVELS OF THE ATLANTIC AND PA CIFIC OCEANS. The popular notion which had so long prevailed that the Atlantic Ocean was many feet higher than the Pacific at the Isthmus of Panama, has been formally exploded. Colonel Totten lias decided, after a scries of careful tidal observations taken at Panama and Aspinwall Bay, and connected by accurate levels along the line of railroad, that the mean height of the two oceans is exactly the same; although, owing to the difference in the ri-e of tide of both places, there are, of course, times when one of the oceans is higher or lower than the other ; but their mean level, that is to say, their height half-tide, at is now proved to be precisely the same.
