A New Russian Pi.ot. þÿ Austria has found an heir lor the throne of Greece ! Austria proposes that King ( Mho shall adopt | the son of the Duke of Leuchtenberg and | of the Grand Duchess Mary, sister of the present Emperor. This young Prince, aged fifteen years, is also connected with the French Emperor, for he is the grand- J son of Eugene Beauharnois. Should the j Austrian proposal be accepted, it would render Greece more than ever Russian. | The object of Austria cannot he doubted for a moment. She wants to disarm Russian resentment, which burns fiercely against the ungrateful ally, of who re mid the conquest and restoration Hungary by the desertion of Nicholas in his hour of need. As the proposal is flattering to the Emperor Napoleon his Majesty's adhesion ! to the scheme is expected. Thus Austria satisfies and pleases both Russia and Fiance. The Government of Vienna is artfully and quietly preparing schemes ot partition, in the hope of helping themselves to the objects they covet, while offering to others 'what they think would he profitable or I agreeable to have ; and then, when the difficulties begin, the copartners will, as in j the case of Poland, he bound to support each other. The protege of Austria is of the Greek religion, which is, of course, a I great point in his favour. þÿ Letter from | Laris.

The renewal of hostilities between the Turks and Montenegrins is causing uneasiness to the Austrian Government, which, says the German Journal of Frankfort, is considering means to terminate these periodical troubles. This statement, however, is in contradiction to a second, to which tlie same journal proceeds, namely, that tlio Austrian Government will recommend a new circumscription of the Montenegrin frontier at the expense of Turkey. An extension of territory such as, it seems, Austria is prepared to propose has been the aim of all these savage Montenegrin wars of which we constantly hear, aud nothing would be so certain to perpetuate them as to show the mountain robbers that they have discovered the method of success We are told, on the authority before mentioned, that

tbe massacres lately committed by tbe Montenegrins have excited universal horror in Vienna ; but surely the Emperor of Austria, who has in Dalmatia an army commanded by a Field Marshal, can protect the feelings of his suljects without seeking to despoil the Sultan, his neighbour. (From the Grenada Chronicle, September 20.) Tobago. þÿ We mentioned, three weeks since, the sudden change which had taken place in the administratorship of the Government of Tobago, when Mr. Keens, senior member of the Executive Committee was nominated under the royal sign manual to supersede Mr. Kirk, President of the Legislative Council in the administration which had devolved on him in the absence of the Lieutenant-Governor according to the old rule. Our Tobago advices by the last mail report a break up of the ministry as the consequence of the slight thus cast upon Mr. Kirk. Messrs. James Leith and S. H. F. Abbott, as well as Mr. Kirk, of the Executive Committee, had tendered their resignation to the Administrator of the Government, with the full sympathy and approval of an influential section of the community, dissatisfied at the summary insult assumed to have been given the superseded Administrator ; and a new ministry had been formed, composed of Mr. Robert Gordon, from the Council, and Messrs. G. B. Van Buren (Solicitor General), and John Leith, of the Assembly. It is stated in the Tobago Chronicle of the 5th instant, that this Executive Committee met on the 4th, when, our contemporary presumes, that matters connected with the session of the Legislature which was to open on the 9th were considered, but what, those matters were it is not stated. On the 6th there was to be a Privy Council. þÿ So, says the Tobago Chronicle , þÿ matters are progressing lavourably."

Although in the abstract this mode ot reasoning and acting may be considered have right by many, it increase of being generous or liberal, certainly cannot be said to and its the merit at policy, least, in some instances, may fully be questioned þÿ ivarice often defeats itself. Formerly the merchants of this Island sold the provisions, candles, &e., which they imported to consumers, or to those persons who were in the habit of endeavouring to make a living by retailing out such goods in the smallest quantities. Such, however, I regret to say, is not the course always pursued in the present day, ior, I find some merchants in addition to their ostensible line of businessþÿ importing merchants þÿ have also opened þÿ Huckster retailing their Pork, þÿshops forthe purpose the Candles, &c., by of stiver, thus depriving of their legitimate gains that numerous class of people who unfortunately, in the paucity of other resources, are compelled by the impoverished circumstances of the country to adopt this mode in order to eke out a support for themselves and families þÿ for, of course, the importer can under-sell the Huckster, out of whom lie has already made a profit. j The official notice published this day by the ; Secretary of the Government in connection i with the health of the Island, affords us the j opportunity once again of shewing the Island | as being perfectly healthy, and with a certainty, we hope, of continuing so. Our Windward Island files have reached us in due course. From their contents we make a few extracts. At Trinidad the Cholera is reported to have reappeared, but other accounts contradict its existence. The Authorities of Grenada had adopted every sanitory measure to prevent, if possible, the introduction again of that fatal disease into that Island. Porto Rico is said to be suffering to an inconceivable extent from the effects of the same Epidemic; at Ponce the disease þÿ knows no þÿdistinction, numbering among its victims some persons from this Island. While we rejoice that one of our sister-islands (St. Thomas) is entirely rid of the malady, and trust that a removal of the existing quarantine between us may he speedily effected, we have the painful intelligence that the other sister-island (St. Johns) is the scene of much woe, owing to the ascendant prevalence of the disease there. We now turn to our extracts, some of which are of : a more pleasing tendency : ANTIGUA. þÿ We copy the following Address presented to the newly-appointed Chief Judge, and His þÿHonor manly s and unostentatious Reply in acknowledgment of the compliment, from the Grenada Chronicle þÿ and which go far to shew the cordial feelings that are likely to exist between the new Judge and the Antiguans : þÿ j ADDRESS OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL : þÿ May it please your Honour, þÿ I pray leave to tender you, on behalf of the Bar, a cordial welcome to the Bench of Antigua, and to assure your Honour that we congratulate our-

selves and the community at large, that a Gentleman of your distinguished attainments, and a Barrister of your high standing and acknowledged reputation, has been selected by His Excellency to act as our Chief Justice. þÿ I desire to add, that it will he at all times the anxious desire of my learned friend and

myself humbly to cooperate with your Honor in the discharge of the responsible duties at taching to your high þÿoffice. REPLY OF THE CHIEF JUSTICE. þÿ I tender you my best thanks for your address, and for the cordial welcome with which you have received and honoured me on this the first occasion of my presiding in this Court. I accept it with feelings of pleasure, as an honourable prelude to those engagements and duties on which we are mutually about to enter, and as a public testimony of our united desire to sustain those institutions which are established for the general welfare of society. þÿ When the Governor of this ancient and loyal colony proposed to recommend me to our Gracious Sovereign for the appointment to which His Excellency has been pleased provisionally to appoint me, I could not reply, as did þÿ the Shunamite to the similar question þÿ Wouldst thou be spoken for to the King þÿ1 þÿ that I dwelt among my own people ; for I dwelt in a land which was not my own, and among a people. with whom I was not connected, but yet among a people whom I loved, and was willing to serve ; and I accepted this appointment, as I deemed it was my duty to do so. þÿ I have not so acted from the vain motive of worldly honour ; and I come among you without partialities to gratify or private interests to serve. þÿ I have happily too long been connected with the profession of the Law not to he fully sensible of the assistance which can be rendered by an enlightened and independent Bar to the

Judge ; and I rejoice to think that I shall be associated with you, Mr. Attorney-General, and the Gentlemen of this Bar. þÿ Myself connected with the Colonial Bar, I trust that my elevation, without political interest, to the judicial seat, will encourage pa rents in these colonies to educate some of their sons for that honourable profession, and stimulate the young men who have entered or shall enter upon that career to the industry and emulation without which no man should expect to succeed. þÿ In my humble endeavours to administer impartial justice I shall hope to obtain such success, and such success only, as shall promote the Glory of God and the good of this þÿpeople. ST. KITTS. þÿ In the House of Assembly of this Island a Bill had been passed to include the Cape de Verd Islands among the places whence immigrants may he imported. JAMAICA. þÿ A Comet, supposed to he the Great Comet of 1856, had been seen at Jamaica lately. This meteor made its appearance near the belt of Orion, in an easterly direction, shewing in its course its brilliant tail, and af terwards remained stationary as a beautiful light in the heavens, eclipsing all the stars in brilliancy. þÿ þÿ

Theft. þÿ On Sunday night last the house of Mr. W. Branagen, painter, of this town, was broken into, and a small box containing about $60 in coin stolen from a press in the room. The box has since been recovered near the premises with $9 and some cents in it.
Saturday, the 25th instant, being the end of our Hurricane Season, which we have happily so far passed over in safety, the day will be observed as a holy-day.

From the London Weekly Dispatch. THE RUSSIAN MISUNDERSTANDING. The Vienna correspondent of The Times of Friday supplies an interesting explanation of the frontier dispute ; þÿ þÿ The 20th article of the treaty of peace concluded at Paris iu the mouth ot March last, can hardly fail the to Allied between lead to a serious misutideistaudiug Powers and Russia, should the latter object to its beiug somewhat modified. The question at issue is oue of great importance. Wheu Austria proposed to her Allies entirely to remove Russia from the Danube, it was agreed that the new frontier between Russia aud Moldavia should be formed by a line, which beginning in the neighbourhood ot Chotyut, aud following the line ot mountains runuing at towards the South-East, should terminate Lake Salzyk þÿ If the original idea had been oi carried out, Russia would have ceded two-thirds Bessarabia to Moldavia ; but when the question of the ratification of the frontier was discussed at Paris, the Russian diplomatists spoke in such strong terms of the unnecessary humiliation to which their couutry would be subjected, should such a large cession of territory be made, that the representatives of the Allies eventually agreed to the following conditions: þÿ The new frontier shall begin at the Black Sea, at one kilometre to the East of the lake Bourna Sola, shall iu a straight line join the load to Aokermann, shall follow that road as far as the valley of Trajan, shall pass the South of Bolgrad, shall ascend the river Yalpuck as far

as the heights of Saratsika, and shall end at Kotamori, on þÿPruth. þÿ According to the Russian maps produced at is Conference, there was terra firmabetween Bolgrad aud the Lake of Yalpuck, but in reality such is not the case. The English, French and Austrian members ot the Frontier | Commission declare that the object of the Allied Powers will not be attained unless Bolgrad is given to Moldavia, but the Russian Government has suddenly discovered that the place iu question, which, according to all accouuts, is a miserable nest, is of great strategic importance, and refused to cede it As has been said, it was and is the object of the Allies entirely to remove Russia from the Dauube, but if Article 20 of the treaty is carried out to the letter they will not attiiu it, as Bolgrad lies on the lake of Yalpuck. which is connected with the Kilia arm of the Danube by means of the Lake of Kagurlin and the Repida river. It may be remarked that the Repida river falls into the Danube close to the important fortress of Ismail. A very active diplomatic correspondence is now going on respecting Bolgrad, and the Russians may probably be induced to cede it, if France docs her duty towards her Allies The British and Austrian Governments are said to be extremely indignant at the bad faith of Russia, who previously to the signature of the treaty of peace must have been as well aware as she is now that no line of demarcation can be drawn between Bolgrad and the lake of þÿYalpuck.

TURKEY The Oesterreichische Zeitung has received news of importance from Cattaro. The Turkish steamers Malakoff and Siiistria, with Mehemed Pacha, the Turkish Governor-General of Bosnia, and four battalions of Guards, on board, are expected at Antivari, in Albania. DIGNITY OF MANHOOD That some men in the world should be richer than others is natural and is necessary, and could only be prevented by gross violations of right. Leave men to the free use of their powers, and some will accumulate more than their neighbours. But, to be prosperous is not to be superior, and should form no barrier between men. Wealth ought not to secure to the prosperous the slightest consideration. The only distinctions which should be recognized are those of the soul, of strong principle, of incorruptible integrity, of usefulness, of cultivated intellect, of fidelity in seeking for truth. A man, in proportion as he has these claims, should be honoured and welcomed everywhere. We see not why such a man, however coarsely if neatly dressed, should not be a respected guest in the most splendid mansions, and at the most brilliant meetings. A man is worth infinitely more than the saloons, and the costumes, and the show of the universe. He was made to tread all these beneath his feet,. What an insult to hu anity is the present, deference to dress and upholstery, as if silkworms, and looms, and scissors, and needles, could produce something nobler than a man ! Every good man should protest against a caste (bunded on outward prosperity, because it exalts the outward above the inward, the material above the spiritual; because ii pritigs from and cherishes a contemptible pride in superficial and transitory distinctions ; because it alienates man li on his brother, breaks the tie of common humanity, and
breeds jealousy, scorn and mutual ill-will. Can this be needed to social order?

AMERICAN WASHING MACHINE. An exceedingly ingenious and useful domestic implement is now being exhibited in London, on the premises of Mr. B. Moore, an American, by which an entirely new, easy, and efficient mode of washing all kinds of garments and fabrics is substituted for the tedious and laborious process by hand in use from time immemorial. The essential characteristic of the invention consists in the employment of floating balls in the operation of washing. Some 200 or 300 of these balls, each of which is about the size of a Seville orange, and made of elm wood, are put in a wooden trough, two or 1 three feet long by fifteen inches deep, containing water or soapsuds, in which they all float. A fulcrum is placed at the back of the trough, having a cross beam attached to it resembling a common pump handle. On one side of the fulcrum an apparatus like a small window sash, to which the clothes to be washed are fastened, is suspended from the crossbeam immediately over the mouth of the trough, and at the extreme end of the beam, on the opposite side of the fulcrum, is a box into which weight may be put until it slightly weighs
the operation moves the , beam-handle up and down as if she were
immerse the sash laden with clothes among j the balls and suds, and move it about

breaking or tearing off buttons, effectually removes every trace of dirt in an incredibly few minutes, and the operation is complete. The labour required is so slight that a child from twelve to fourteen years of age may perform it with ease. The action

: ordinary threefold process of pounding. rubbing and squeezing, and as it can never exceed the resistance offered by the floating balls, it is thereby kept within bounds which are perfectly safe for the most delicate fabrics, the wear and tear being indeed, less than in ordinary washing by hand. The machine was exhibited at the Paris Exhibition, where it attached considerable interest, and numbers were sold, the Duchess of Sutherland, who bought no fewer than four, being among the purchasers.
